title: Culture Plate
pitch: A glowing petri dish under a blacklight holds a live Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion culture. The visitor inoculates it with a fingertip, then steers its chemistry by dragging a marker across a hand-labelled feed/kill map whose regions are named like pantry items (spots, worms, coral, bubbling, mitosis). A slow drift mode lets the culture ferment from one regime to the next, and a poster mode stamps the result with a museum-style specimen label and a shareable seed.
whyNow: Timeless: reaction-diffusion is a very photogenic bit of mathematics, and an ultraviolet blacklight palette with a lab-specimen framing and pantry-named regimes gives it a point of view that differs from the existing explorers.

research.summary: Gray-Scott is a two-chemical model on a grid: chemical A is fed in at rate f, chemical B is removed at rate k, and B converts A. Per Karl Sims's tutorial as seen in a search result, the Laplacian is a 3x3 convolution with centre -1, edges 0.2 and corners 0.05 (summing to zero), and a typical starting pair is f=0.055, k=0.062; an independent write-up (Algosome) gives the same kernel. The (f, k) plane is a map of regimes (spots, loops, solitons, worms, mazes, stripes, waves, solid regions), but published example coordinates disagree between sources because grid size, diffusion constants and initial conditions differ, so the page will calibrate its own map, label presets as this page's calibration and test each by running the core headless. Prior art is closer than first assumed: Karl Sims's RD Tool already offers a clickable pattern map of feed and kill (it needs WebGL 2 with a float colour-buffer extension), Google Experiments has a Gray-Scott toy with feed and kill controls, and student projects offer sliders and named presets. The value therefore lies in the point of view: pantry-named regions, ferment-drift, local chemistry brushes, specimen-label poster and a shareable seed. Model limits: a toy two-species chemistry on a flat grid, not real fermentation. On biology the page stays cautious: Turing-type mechanisms are discussed for zebrafish stripes, but the literature disagrees on the molecular basis and on whether classic reaction-diffusion applies, and much other support is resemblance to simulations.

sources.title: Reaction-Diffusion Tutorial (Karl Sims)
sources.snippet: Tutorial describing chemical A fed at rate f and chemical B removed at rate k on a grid, with a 3x3 Laplacian kernel and suggested starting values for diffusion, feed and kill.
sources.note: Found again in a claim search whose result states the 3x3 kernel (centre -1, edges 0.2, corners 0.05) and f=0.055, k=0.062; WebFetch of www.karlsims.com failed (DNS), so the page was not opened. The kernel is also confirmed by the independent Algosome result. DA and DB values were not re-seen.

sources.title: Reaction Diffusion: The Gray-Scott Algorithm (Algosome)
sources.snippet: Independent write-up giving the same 3x3 kernel (centre -1, edges 0.2, corners 0.05) and explaining the multiply-and-sum step per neighbour.
sources.note: Found again; independent write-up agreeing on the kernel; also reports f=0.0545, k=0.062 giving fingerprint-like patterns (single source, not used as a fact).

sources.title: Pearson classes (Robert Munafo, xmorphia)
sources.snippet: Page on the extended Pearson classification of Gray-Scott patterns by feed rate F and kill rate k (found again in a search for the claim; page not opened).
sources.note: Found again by a claim search; supports that Gray-Scott patterns are classified over the (F, k) plane. The specific kill-axis sentence in the scout's snippet was not seen, so it is not used.

sources.title: Pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems using the Gray-Scott model (Univ. Frankfurt student project)
sources.snippet: Student project with slider-based feed/kill controls, paint-on-canvas and named presets; lists example (F,k) pairs for solitons, worms, spots and loops, and mazes.
sources.note: Found again twice; example numbers differ from another source seen (e.g. solitons and spots both quoted near F=0.030, k=0.062 by different sources), which supports the calibration risk

sources.title: RDTool example Reaction-Diffusion Explorer Tool (Karl Sims)
sources.snippet: Help page for an interactive Gray-Scott explorer with presets and drawing controls; needs WebGL 2 with a float colour-buffer extension.
sources.note: Found again; browser Gray-Scott explorer where the pattern map is clicked (feed vertical, kill roughly horizontal); needs WebGL 2 plus EXT_color_buffer_float per the result. Closest prior art to the named-map idea.

sources.title: Gray-Scott Simulation (Google Experiments)
sources.snippet: Google Experiments Gray-Scott solver where users draw living cells and set feed and death rates, with presets.
sources.note: Found again; second independent piece of prior art. Creator and 2013 date appeared in one result only and are not used.

sources.title: PMC3303118 (article on Turing-type mechanisms in vertebrate development; title and authors not confirmed)
sources.snippet: Page text seen via search: simulations of reaction-diffusion replicate zebrafish stripes, shells, teeth, digits and follicle spacing; few systems allow experimental tests and much literature relies on resemblance to simulations; reports a tested palate-ridge case (FGF and Shh).
sources.note: Found again twice. The scout labelled it a 2011 review; type, title and year were not confirmed, so it is cited only for the cautious wording about resemblance and scarce tests.

sources.title: Pigment cell movement is not required for generation of Turing patterns in zebrafish skin (Bullara and De Decker, Nature Communications)
sources.snippet: Abstract mirrored across several sites: zebrafish skin patterns arise from a Turing bifurcation without cell motion, via differential growth, differing from the classic reaction-diffusion mechanism.
sources.note: Title corrected (the scout's title was not the paper's); authors, journal and 2015 confirmed by several results

sources.title: Complex Patterns in a Simple System (Pearson, 1993)
sources.snippet: Pearson's Gray-Scott pattern catalogue; seen in a search result, which notes it used a single starting pattern.
sources.note: Seen in claim-search results; used only to back that the pattern classification originates from Gray-Scott parameter sweeps and that classes depend on initial conditions

sources.title: Studies of Turing pattern formation in zebrafish skin (PMC8580470)
sources.snippet: Review of Turing studies in zebrafish skin; result text mentions debate on whether the classic mechanism applies because pigment cells move and touch.
sources.note: Seen in search results; year not confirmed. Independent source showing the zebrafish mechanism is still debated

facts.claim: In the Gray-Scott model chemical A is fed in at rate f and chemical B removed at rate k; the common 3x3 Laplacian kernel has centre -1, edges 0.2 and corners 0.05 (sum zero), and f=0.055, k=0.062 is a typical starting pair.
Gray-Scott patterns are classified over the feed (F) and kill (k) plane into named regimes such as spots, loops, solitons, worms and mazes.

Published example (F,k) values for the named regimes are not consistent across sources and depend on grid, diffusion constants and initial conditions, so the page labels its map as its own calibration.

Interactive Gray-Scott explorers already exist: Karl Sims's RD Tool (clickable feed/kill pattern map, needs WebGL 2 with a float colour-buffer extension), a Google Experiments toy with feed and kill controls, and student-project sliders with presets.

Zebrafish stripes are discussed as Turing-type patterns, but the literature disagrees on the mechanism (for example a bifurcation without cell motion versus a doubt that classic reaction-diffusion applies), and much support elsewhere is resemblance to simulations.

design.coreLoop: Seed a dish with a fingertip, pick a spot on the feed/kill map, watch the culture settle into a regime, then nudge, drift or contaminate it to see it transform. The map is the second-minute reward (each region behaves differently and has a name), drift mode and the contamination brush are the tenth-minute reward (staged mishaps make new hybrids), and the poster button gives a keepable specimen print with a seed in the URL hash.
sophisticationHooks: Hand-calibrated feed/kill map with named regimes and a draggable marker, plus a ferment-drift mode that slowly walks the marker along a path across regimes
Brush tools that act locally on chemistry: inoculate (add B), nutrient spill (add A), poison (raise kill), so mishaps become compositional tools
Specimen-poster export: ultraviolet palette, generated catalogue number and Latin-style name derived deterministically from f, k and seed, with the full state in the URL hash
Pure numerical core (init, step, state, reset) running fixed timesteps with seeded noise in a worker, a mass-conservation-style sanity clamp and no NaN reaching the canvas
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: Gray-Scott core on a 256x256 grid (192x192 fallback if frame time exceeds budget) in an inline Blob worker with a main-thread fallback (CSP allows worker-src 'self' blob:), about 8 steps per frame; canvas2d palette renderer with 3 colour ramps; feed/kill map canvas with about 10 to 12 named regions and a draggable marker; inoculate, nutrient and poison brushes; drift mode along a fixed path; URL hash state (f, k, seed, palette, painted dots); PNG poster export with generated catalogue number and Latin-style name; keyboard control of the marker and brushes; light/dark and reduced-motion handling; about/making-of panel listing sources. Cut: WebGL path, 3D view, audio, saved galleries. Timebox: core plus map first, then brushes and drift, poster last; if short on time, drop one ramp and the nutrient brush.
risks: Preset f,k coordinates vary between sources and implementations; the page labels regions as its own calibration and a headless run of the core checks each named region before shipping.

Prior art is close: Karl Sims's RD Tool already has a clickable feed/kill pattern map, so differentiation depends on pantry-named regions, drift mode, brushes and poster polish rather than on the simulation or the map itself.
Pearson's Greek-letter class labels were seen in a search result but the page still uses its own names and does not cite Pearson's letters.
The DA and DB diffusion values were not re-seen in a result; the page tunes them in its own headless calibration and does not attribute them to a source.
CPU simulation on low-end phones: start at 256x256 and drop to 192x192 if frame time exceeds budget.

Biology line in the about panel stays cautious (discussed for zebrafish stripes, mechanism debated, much support is resemblance to simulations); the page says it is a toy chemistry, not real fermentation. The page shows the zebrafish line as 'as of 2026-10-10, per' the cited papers, or omits it.
The scout's title and year for PMC3303118 could not be confirmed, so the about panel cites it only by its PMC identifier or omits it.

verification.notes: Kernel, f/k values and the regime map were each found again in independent search results (Sims, Algosome, Frankfurt, Pearson), but no page opened because www.karlsims.com failed DNS; two source titles were corrected and DA/DB values left unverified. Buildable in a morning at 256x256 in a worker, safe and offline, with close prior art so the named map, drift and poster must carry the delight.
